title: Volume 0 · How ERPNext Thinks: The Document Lifecycle
subtitle: Lessons 1–10: draft, submit, cancel and amend, and the audit trail a wrong document leaves behind
outcomes: Explain docstatus 0, 1 and 2 to a client who believes they can edit a submitted invoice
Show exactly which records a submission creates in the stock ledger and the general ledger
Cancel or amend correctly, and say out loud what each one does to the audit trail
Read and demonstrate the system's own Version log when a number is questioned
Recognise the referencing-document error that blocks a cancel, before the client meets it

slides.title: One field, three worlds: draft, submitted, cancelled
bullets: Every document carries a hidden integer called docstatus, and it decides what the document may do
Draft is docstatus 0: fully editable, saves freely, and has no effect on stock or on the books whatsoever
Submitted is docstatus 1: frozen, and submission is the moment stock moves and the ledger posts
Cancelled is docstatus 2: the record stays, its postings are reversed, and nothing is ever deleted
A consultant who teaches this first spends the rest of the project answering fewer angry messages

rows: Stock → Delivery Note → New, add any item
Form shows Draft at the top right
Name assigned, status still Draft, stock balance unchanged
Open Stock Balance for the item
Quantity identical to before the draft existed
Return to the note and click Submit
Status changes to Submitted and the document locks
Quantity has now dropped by the delivered amount
Status becomes Cancelled and the quantity returns

slides.notes: Run this in front of the client, do not describe it. The moment that lands is step three: the draft exists, it looks finished, and the stock has not moved. Say the sentence out loud that you want repeated in the office — a draft is a proposal, submitting is the commit. Every argument later in the project about 'the system got it wrong' starts with someone assuming a draft did something.

slides.title: Submission is the commit: one click, four records
bullets: A submitted Delivery Note writes a Stock Ledger Entry that reduces the Bin quantity and computes cost of goods sold
It writes a General Ledger pair: cost of goods sold debited, stock in hand credited, at the same value
It writes a Payment Ledger-adjacent effect only later, when the invoice claims the revenue, not here
Nothing is written while the document is a draft, which is why an unsubmitted pile is invisible to reports
Teach the client to look for the ledger rows, not the document status, when they doubt a posting

rows: Stock Ledger Entry exists for the note
Stock → Stock Ledger, filter by voucher
Accounts → General Ledger, filter by voucher

slides.notes: The four-line check is what separates a consultant from a trainer. Anyone can say 'submit it'; you are showing the client the two ledgers and the bin disagreeing with their mental model at exactly the same instant, by the same amount. If a client ever reports a wrong stock figure, the first question is always the same: was the document submitted, and can you show me the voucher?

slides.title: Cancel reverses; it does not delete
bullets: Cancelling a submitted document writes offsetting entries rather than removing the original ones
The document keeps its name, its date, its owner and its links, so the story of what happened survives
The stock comes back and the ledger is balanced back to zero, but the history now includes both attempts
A cancelled document still appears in searches and in the Version log, which is exactly what an auditor wants
Say the phrase early: we never delete, we reverse — deleting is reserved for drafts nobody submitted

rows: Open the Stock Ledger for the item
Two rows: the original and its reversal
Open the General Ledger for the voucher
Four rows: the original pair and the reversal pair
Quantity back to 50, but the history is longer

slides.notes: Clients ask for delete because their spreadsheet let them. Show them the reversal rows and the argument ends: the stock is back, the books balance, and the record of the mistake is permanent in exactly the way statutory audit wants. The only document that should ever be deleted is a draft — and even then, explain that cancelling is safer.

slides.title: Amend creates a linked copy, not an edit
bullets: Amend is only offered on a cancelled document: cancel first, then amend, in that order, always
The new document carries amended_from pointing at the original, which is how the chain is reconstructed
The original stays cancelled and untouched, so the pair tells the truth about the correction
Amending a submitted document without cancelling is impossible by design, not by configuration
Version numbers climb in the name, so three attempts read as three documents with a visible lineage

rows: Open the new note, Connections tab

slides.notes: The habit to install is cancel, then amend, in that order, and never 'edit and save' on something submitted. When the client asks why they cannot simply fix the quantity, the answer is the ledger: the submitted rows are already in the stock and the books, and correcting them by editing would leave no trace of what was posted. Amendment keeps both halves of the story.

slides.title: The few fields a submitted document still allows
bullets: Some fields are flagged Allow on Submit, and those stay editable after the document is committed
Supplier bill number and bill date on a Purchase Invoice are the classic examples consultants rely on
Shipping address and contact details can often be corrected without unwinding a stock movement
The flag is per field, per doctype, so the honest answer is 'check this field', not 'check the document'
Anything that changes money or quantity is never allow-on-submit, because the ledger already posted

rows: Tick box on the field definition
Version log entry with old and new

slides.notes: This lesson prevents the most common support ticket in the first month: 'the field is greyed out'. Rather than promising that documents are editable, teach the client that a committed document is frozen except where somebody deliberately allowed a field, and that the correction will appear in the Version log. Then show them the Version log so the promise is visibly true.

slides.title: Why a cancel sometimes refuses: active references
bullets: A document cannot be cancelled while another submitted document points at it as its source
A Delivery Note with a submitted Sales Invoice against it will refuse cancellation, with a named reason
The message names the blocking documents, so the fix is a sequence of cancels from the bottom up
This is a feature, not a bug: it stops an invoice existing for goods that were never delivered
Teach the direction of the chain: order, then delivery, then invoice, then payment, cancelled in reverse

rows: Submit a Delivery Note from a Sales Order
Create and submit a Sales Invoice from it
Invoice submitted, linked to the note
Try to cancel the Delivery Note
Red error naming Active Referencing Documents
The invoice name is listed as the blocker

slides.notes: Expect this error in the first week of every go-live, always in the same shape: someone wants to undo a delivery and cannot. Walk the chain out loud — the invoice exists because the delivery happened, so the invoice must go first, then the delivery. Clients remember the direction better than they remember the message.

slides.title: Showing a client the system's own memory
bullets: Every saved change to a document writes a Version entry with the field, the old value and the new value
Comments and assignments sit beside it, so 'who asked for this' has an answer inside the document
The Version log is what you open when a number is questioned and nobody admits to changing it
It is read-only to normal users and cannot be edited from the interface, which is the point
Show it once during training and the 'the system changed my number' conversation largely disappears

rows: Field, old value, new value, user, timestamp
No edit controls on Version rows

slides.notes: This is the slide that buys trust. Instead of claiming the system is auditable, you open a document, change the bill number, and let the Version row appear in front of the client with their own name on it. Then say the sentence they will repeat to their auditor: nothing that matters can be changed without leaving a mark.

slides.title: Amend, cancel, or write a new document?
bullets: Same document, wrong content, nothing downstream yet: cancel, then amend, and keep the chain
Wrong document entirely, nothing referenced: cancel it and raise the correct doctype instead
Downstream documents already exist: unwind from the bottom of the chain, never from the middle
Nothing was ever submitted: edit the draft, or delete it, because no ledger or stock exists
Financial corrections after a closed period go through journals, not by touching the original

rows: Open it and correct the field
Wrong customer on a submitted invoice
Journal entry in the open period

slides.notes: Give the client a decision table rather than a lecture. The four rows here cover almost every correction they will face in the first quarter, and the closed-period row is the one that saves an argument with the auditor. Say plainly that journals are not a loophole: they are the documented way to correct a period that has been reported.

slides.title: Reports only believe submitted documents
bullets: The General Ledger, the Stock Ledger and the financial statements read submitted records only
A draft invoice is absent from receivables ageing, so a pile of drafts is a hidden cash-flow gap
Stock Balance counts submitted stock entries, so a draft delivery looks like stock that is still yours
The status filter in a list view is your fastest diagnostic when a total will not reconcile
Agree one reporting rule with the client: nothing counts until it is submitted, and then it always counts
slides.notes: This is where a month-end reconciles or does not. Show the client the ageing report before and after submitting one invoice, then ask them what a hundred unsubmitted invoices would do to their cash forecast. The rule you extract from them — nothing counts until it is submitted — becomes the operating discipline for the whole project.

slides.title: The five-minute lifecycle demo you can give anywhere
bullets: Draft a document, show it does nothing, submit it, show two ledgers move, cancel it, show the reversal
Amend the cancelled document, show the link, then open the Version log and let them read their own name
Finish with the reporting rule: drafts are invisible, submitted is permanent, cancelled is still history
This demo fits in five minutes and answers most objections raised in a requirements workshop
Rehearse it once; the sequence is what makes it land, not the words

rows: Create and save a delivery note
Quantity down, cost of goods sold posted
Reversal rows, new document with amended_from
Field changes with user and timestamp

slides.notes: Keep this demo rehearsed and short. The temptation is to explain docstatus as a database concept; resist it and stay with the four visible moments — draft does nothing, submit posts, cancel reverses, amend links. If you can deliver this in five minutes without notes, you can open almost any ERPNext workshop without losing the room.

lab.title: Lab · Prove the lifecycle on Seri Murni's stock
steps: Open a new Delivery Note for Aeon Big, item SM-BL200 qty 5 from Main Warehouse, and save without submitting
Record the Stock Balance for SM-BL200 and confirm the draft has not changed it
Submit the note, then read the Stock Ledger row and the two General Ledger rows for that voucher
Confirm cost of goods sold of 600.00 at 120.00 per unit and that gross profit is unaffected until invoiced
Cancel the note, then read the reversal rows in both ledgers and confirm the quantity is restored
Amend the cancelled note, change the quantity to 4, submit it and confirm amended_from points at the original
Open the Version log on the amended document and report every field change with its user and timestamp
Create a Sales Invoice from the amended note, submit it, then attempt to cancel the note and read the blocker error
Cancel the invoice first and then the note, and confirm the chain unwinds bottom-up without a ledger imbalance
lab.done: The candidate can show a draft that moved nothing, a submission that posted to two ledgers, a cancellation that reversed rather than deleted, an amendment chained by amended_from, and the exact error text of a blocked cancel.

quiz.question: A client wants to correct the quantity on a submitted Delivery Note. What is the correct instruction?
options: Edit the row and save, since quantity is allow-on-submit
Cancel the note, then amend it, because submission already posted stock and cost
Delete the note and create a fresh one to keep the books clean
Ask a System Manager to unlock docstatus in the database
quiz.why: A submitted document is frozen because its Stock Ledger and General Ledger rows already exist. Cancel reverses those rows and amend creates a linked copy, which is the only correction that keeps the audit trail honest.

quiz.question: What happens to stock when a Delivery Note is saved as a draft?
options: Stock is reserved and projected quantity drops, actual quantity unchanged
Nothing at all: no stock ledger entry is written until submission
Stock drops immediately and is restored if the draft is discarded
Stock drops only if the item is not batch-tracked
quiz.why: Draft documents post nothing. Projected quantity on a Sales Order is a different mechanism; on a draft Delivery Note there is neither stock movement nor ledger effect, which is why unsubmitted work is invisible to reports.

quiz.question: A Delivery Note refuses to cancel and names an active referencing document. What does that mean?
options: The document is locked by another user editing it right now
A submitted Sales Invoice points at the note, so the invoice must be cancelled first
The stock is negative and must be corrected before cancelling
The note was amended and only the amendment can be cancelled
quiz.why: ERPNext blocks cancellation while a submitted document references the note, because otherwise an invoice would exist for goods that were never delivered. The chain unwinds from the bottom: invoice, then delivery.

quiz.question: Where do you prove that a field was changed and by whom?
options: In the document's comments, if somebody wrote it down
In the Version log, which records field, old value, new value, user and time
In the Stock Ledger, since every change produces a row
In the browser history of the user who made the change
quiz.why: Every saved change writes a Version entry with the field, the previous and new value, the user and the timestamp. It is read-only in the interface, which is what makes it usable as audit evidence.

quiz.question: A hundred Sales Invoices are sitting as drafts at month end. What does the receivables ageing show?
options: All hundred, because the invoice exists as a record
None of them, because reports read submitted documents only
Only the ones with a due date inside the period
The total value, but without customer names
quiz.why: Financial and stock reports read submitted records. A pile of drafts is a hidden cash-flow and stock gap, which is why the reporting rule — nothing counts until it is submitted — belongs in the client's operating discipline.

memory.spine: A document does nothing until it is submitted, and after that it is never deleted, only reversed or amended.

device.label: Draft, commit, cancel, amend
expansion: Draft does nothing at all: no stock, no ledger, no report row
Submit is the commit: one click writes the stock ledger and the general ledger
Cancel reverses with offsetting rows and keeps the document for the record
Amend only follows a cancel and links back through amended_from
References block a cancel, so a chain unwinds from the invoice down to the delivery

cards.q: What does saving a draft change in the stock and the books?
cards.a: Nothing. No stock ledger entry and no general ledger row exists until the document is submitted, so drafts are invisible to reports.

cards.q: Why can a submitted document not simply be deleted?
cards.a: Its stock and ledger rows are already posted. Cancelling writes offsetting rows and keeps the record, which is what an auditor needs to see.

cards.q: What must happen before a document can be amended?
cards.a: It must be cancelled first. Amend then creates a new document carrying amended_from, while the original stays cancelled and untouched.

cards.q: What does the error Active Referencing Documents tell you to do?
cards.a: A submitted document points at this one, so cancel from the bottom of the chain upwards: invoice first, then delivery note.

cards.q: Which single report check proves a posting really happened?
cards.a: Open the Stock Ledger and the General Ledger filtered by the voucher. If the rows are there, the document posted; if not, it is still a draft.

trap.what: The client asks you to 'just delete' a wrongly submitted invoice so the ageing report looks right.
trap.why: Submitted documents cannot be deleted because their ledger rows already exist. Cancel it, then amend or re-raise, and show the Version log so the correction is visible rather than erased.

narration: Every ERPNext document has three states, and one hidden field decides which state it is in. A draft is a proposal: you can type anything, save it as often as you like, and nothing happens to stock or to the books. A submitted document is a commitment. The single click writes a stock ledger entry and a general ledger pair, and the document freezes. A cancelled document is history: the postings are reversed by offsetting rows, and the record stays exactly where it was. Nothing is deleted, which is why an auditor can follow a mistake from beginning to end. When something is wrong, cancel first and then amend, because amendment is only offered on a cancelled document and it creates a new one linked back through amended_from. If a cancel is refused, look for the active referencing document and unwind the chain from the bottom, invoice before delivery. And remember what reports read: only submitted records. A hundred draft invoices are invisible to receivables ageing. Teach the five minute demo, draft, submit, cancel, amend, and most objections never get raised.
